idiom_name: DbSet<T> + IQueryable over an injected DbContext
implementation_notes: EF Core's DbContext is itself an implementation of Repository and Unit of Work (Microsoft's guidance says so explicitly), so DbSet<T> plus LINQ is the collection-like surface and SaveChangesAsync is the flush. The usual realization is to inject the context into application services and query with IQueryable; add a hand-written repository only where the domain must not see EF types. Use AsNoTracking and projections on read paths, and never let IQueryable escape the application layer.
pitfalls: Wrapping DbContext one-to-one duplicates the repository it already implements and blocks EF features (compiled queries, bulk updates, Include tuning); do it only for a real domain boundary.
DbContext is not thread-safe and must be scoped per request or unit of work; sharing it across tasks corrupts the change tracker.
A repository method that calls SaveChangesAsync internally commits half a business operation; keep the flush at the application-service boundary.

variants.name: Hand-written IRepository over the change tracker (DDD style)
variants.idiom_name: IOrderRepository in the domain layer, OrderRepository over DbContext in infrastructure
variants.implementation_notes: Define the interface in the domain layer (IOrderRepository : IRepository<Order>) and implement it in infrastructure over DbContext; the implementation queries with LINQ and mutates aggregates, while SaveChangesAsync stays with the unit of work so the repository never commits per call. This is the eShopOnContainers shape and gives a mockable seam for domain unit tests, at the cost of hiding EF-specific power behind the interface and of one more class per aggregate.
pitfalls: Two layers must agree on aggregate boundaries: a repository that returns entity graphs across aggregates creates accidental coupling that EF will happily cascade.
Returning EF entities with lazy or tracked state hands write capability to callers; project to domain values where the aggregate must not be mutated outside its root.
Generic base repositories that constrain T to an aggregate root are useful, but a repository per table reappears easily once the constraint is dropped for convenience.
